Controlled Opposition.short_definition: A protest group, critic or movement that is secretly funded, steered or shaped by the very power it appears to oppose, so dissent goes somewhere harmless.
Controlled Opposition.expanded_definition: Controlled opposition is resistance that looks independent but is quietly guided by the party it claims to challenge. Instead of banning dissent, the target is offered an official-looking outlet, such as a licensed protest, a friendly critic or a talking shop, where anger is released and nothing changes. The claim needs evidence like money, shared staff or coordination. A critic who is cautious, or a movement that fights over tactics, shows none of that.
Controlled Opposition.plain_language_summary: The people who seem to be fighting something are actually helping it. Your anger gets a place to go, but the place was built so that it never leads to change.
Controlled Opposition.why_this_matters: If you pour your energy into a channel built to absorb it, you can spend years believing you are pushing for change while nothing moves. It can also make you distrust real allies. Asking for evidence protects you from both mistakes.
what_it_is: A group set up, funded or advised by the institution it criticizes, while presenting itself as an independent voice.
An existing movement quietly co-opted, for example by giving its leaders paid roles, access or praise in return for softer demands.
A permitted outlet for dissent, such as a consultation or a hotline, whose results are never allowed to bind anyone.
A pattern in which strong language is used on safe targets while the central power is left alone.
A claim that needs documents, money trails or testimony. A hunch that opposition looks too tidy does not count.
what_it_sounds_like: The petition got a million names and a meeting with the minister, and then a statement that the minister 'heard the concerns'.
A spokesperson thunders about waste and rudeness in the agency, but never mentions the contract that actually decides things.
Funding records show the 'grassroots' watchdog's biggest donor is the company it reports on.
The group's leader meets the people in charge in private, then returns and asks followers to calm down and wait.
Every consultation ends the same way: a thank-you, a report, and no change to the plan.
The rival campaign that proposed a harder demand was ignored by the 'main' opposition and called unrealistic.
The march route, slogans and speakers were all approved by the authorities in advance.
what_it_is_not: Movements argue about tactics all the time. A moderate wing and a radical wing can both be sincere.
A critic who is cautious by temperament or conviction is not a plant. Mildness is not evidence of control.
Overlap between a critic's positions and the interests of those they criticize is common and usually coincidental.
Accepting a meeting, a grant or a seat at a table can be a real strategy, and sometimes it wins concessions.
A group that fails to win is usually just weak or outnumbered. Losing does not prove it was set up to lose.
A group that takes public money for a narrow, openly stated purpose is not secretly steered.
this_may_be_it_when: Documents or reporting show money, staff or direction passing from the target to its 'opponent'.
The opposition's demands shrink each time the target faces real pressure.
Critics who press for binding change are pushed out or discredited by the main opposition, not by the target.
The loudest criticism lands only on issues the target would happily lose.
Several former insiders independently describe being told what to say or leave out.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The group's accounts are public and no link to the target appears in them.
Members openly fight over strategy and the leadership loses votes it wanted to win.
The group has won at least one concession the target resisted.
The critic's mild approach was the same before they had any contact with the target.
The only reason to suspect them is that they disagree with you about tactics.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A movement that prefers negotiation will naturally look soft to those who prefer confrontation.
A leader who meets officials privately may be bargaining in good faith, and may need confidentiality to do it.
Two groups with similar aims may end up sounding alike simply because they read the same research.
common_false_positives: A union leader who settles for a smaller raise than the members hoped, after a vote.
A columnist who criticizes a government's style but agrees with its policy, because that is what they actually believe.
A protest the police helped organize for safety reasons, with nobody steering its message.
discernment_questions: What documents, money trails or named witnesses exist, and who other than the person making the claim has seen them?
Has this group ever won something the target did not want to give?
Could the same behavior be explained by plain caution, disagreement or weakness?
Am I treating every moderate voice as compromised, whatever the facts?
What would I expect to see if this opposition were truly independent, and do I see it?
less_concerning_if: The group publishes its funding and its leaders can be questioned in public.
Its demands have stayed the same while its relations with the target went up and down.
Dissenting members are allowed to speak and to leave without being smeared.
more_concerning_if: Money or personnel links to the target are documented and were not disclosed.
People who propose harder demands are sidelined by the group itself, not by outsiders.
The group advises followers to stop other forms of action while the 'process' runs.
pattern_over_time_signs: Years of consultations, petitions and statements pass with no change in the decision being contested.
The group's language gets milder as its access to the target grows.
Each new burst of public anger is directed to the same safe outlet and then fades.
Independent groups that formed to push harder keep failing to get meetings, funding or coverage.
Controlled Opposition.repair_check: Where a group is found to have taken undisclosed money or direction, repair looks like publishing the whole record, stepping aside and letting members choose new leaders. A fresh logo and a statement about 'lessons learned' with the same people in charge is a different thing.
Controlled Opposition.boundary_respect_check: Watch what happens to a member who asks where the money comes from. Are they answered with figures, or with a cooler welcome? Open books and tolerated questions point one way; hostility to the question points the other.
Controlled Opposition.psychological_mechanism: A sanctioned outlet can feel like progress. Being heard, attending a meeting or signing a petition can release the urge to act, so energy that might have gone into harder options is spent before it builds up. When the visible opponent also seems reasonable and independent, people tend to trust the process and to see impatient critics as extremists.
Controlled Opposition.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe years of effort that ended in a polite report, and a sinking feeling on finding the sponsor behind a trusted group. Some become suspicious of every organization, including honest ones. Others feel foolish, or fall out with friends who stayed involved.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the group a plain question in public or in writing: 'Where does your funding come from, and have you had contact with the agency you are campaigning against?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Make your support depend on evidence: you will give time or money once their accounts and any agreements with the target are published.
response_options.disengagement: Move your effort to another channel, such as a local group with open books, rather than arguing with the leaders of the first one.
response_options.support_seeking: Take what you have found to a journalist, a campaign-finance regulator or a transparency charity, with documents and dates instead of suspicions.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you work for such a group or for the target, record what you were asked to do and when, and raise concerns through your ethics or compliance route.

Controlled Opposition.boundary_script: Verification script (to yourself, before joining or sharing): "Can I name a document, a donor or a witness that shows who steers this group, or am I reacting to a feeling that it is too tidy? Has it ever won anything the other side fought?"
Controlled Opposition.safety_note: Controlled opposition is rarely a personal danger. The risk comes when a group's insiders are pressured, followed or threatened for asking questions, or when you are urged to hand over personal details. If so, stop sharing, save what you hold, and speak to a lawyer, a press-freedom organization or a legal aid service.
misuse_warning: Calling a rival group 'controlled' because it chose a different tactic spreads suspicion without proof and splits movements.
The label can become unfalsifiable: any compromise counts as evidence of control, so no group can ever clear itself.
Controlled Opposition.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Gatekeeping decides who gets in the room at all, while controlled opposition fills the room with a friendly stand-in. Strategic ambiguity hides a speaker's meaning, whereas here the speaker's independence is what is hidden. Information cascades need no planner, because people simply follow each other. This pattern needs someone behind the scenes.
Controlled Opposition.core_meaning: A protest group, critic or movement that is secretly funded, steered or shaped by the very power it appears to oppose, so dissent goes somewhere harmless.

Reputation Laundering.short_definition: Passing a damaging or flattering claim about a person through enough retellings that it loses its source and starts to feel like common knowledge.
Reputation Laundering.expanded_definition: Reputation laundering works like money laundering: the claim goes in dirty and comes out looking clean. A rumor or one disputed incident is repeated by one person, then another, until each listener assumes someone else checked it. Eventually 'everyone knows' it. A single retelling means little, since people pass on gossip carelessly. The pattern shows when the story cannot be traced to anyone who saw it, and when correcting it only makes the retellers repeat it louder.
Reputation Laundering.plain_language_summary: A story about someone gets passed around until nobody remembers who started it, and then people treat it as fact because so many have repeated it.
Reputation Laundering.why_this_matters: The target has to argue against a portrayal with no traceable origin, while each person repeating it treats everyone else's repetition as their evidence for it. You cannot rebut a source that has vanished.
what_it_is: A claim about a person's character that travels from group to group, losing its source with each stop.
Repetition standing in for proof, so that the number of people saying it counts as the evidence.
It can run in reverse, polishing a person's image with praise from people who never dealt with them.
A trail that, when followed carefully, ends at one disputed incident or at no one.
Something that shows up at work, in schools, in families, in congregations and online.
what_it_sounds_like: I don't know the details, but everyone says she's difficult to work with.
That's just what people say about him, there must be something to it.
Three different people warned me about you before I even met you.
I heard it from someone who heard it from the team, so I assume it's true.
It doesn't matter where it started. The reputation is what it is.
Ask anyone in the department. They'll tell you the same thing.
He's got a reputation, so I'd keep your distance.
what_it_is_not: Reputations are often earned. 'Everyone says that' is sometimes simply true.
Several people with similar first-hand experiences who compare notes are corroborating each other. The line to draw is between people who met the person and people who only met the story.
A warning from one colleague who worked with someone and tells you what happened is a report, not laundering.
A person's reputation changing after a documented event, such as a verdict or public statement, is a normal response to news.
A story that is vague because the teller does not remember the details is ordinary gossip.
A formal reference check that asks former managers what they saw.
this_may_be_it_when: You ask anyone repeating the claim what they saw and none of them can say.
When traced back, the claim leads to one disputed incident or to nobody.
The story keeps the same wording from person to person, as though copied.
New people hear the verdict about you before they have met you.
Your corrections are met with 'that's just what people say' instead of a reason.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Several people describe separate first-hand events and can name dates and details.
The claim is traceable to a documented event, such as a finding, a recording or a record.
The people repeating it change their view once they meet you.
The story is specific and the person who knows it is willing to be named.
Different groups who do not know each other reached the same view alone.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People repeat what they heard in good faith, assuming that others had verified it.
A small workplace or town carries news fast and loosely, without anyone meaning harm.
A past mistake may genuinely be part of how someone is remembered, even if the retelling has drifted.
common_false_positives: A new manager warned about a team's morale by a predecessor who handled it first-hand.
A restaurant with a poor reputation because many diners had separate bad meals.
A person who is wary of you because of something you did in front of them, and not something they heard.
discernment_questions: Can any single person say what they personally saw or heard?
Does the claim come back to one source, or do several people have independent experience?
Is the story getting more certain and more detailed than the original facts could support?
If the claim were false, how would anyone in the chain have found out?
Would the same people repeat it to my face, with a chance for me to answer?
less_concerning_if: The people repeating the story can name where they heard it and were not in a hurry to pass it on.
Those who hear your side adjust what they say.
The reputation matches what you can verify from records or from several unconnected people.
more_concerning_if: The story follows you into new jobs, groups or towns where nobody had contact with the original event.
Official-sounding people, such as a manager or an organiser, now repeat it as settled.
Anyone who questions the story is told they are 'taking sides'.
pattern_over_time_signs: Newcomers greet you with a version of the story before you have said a word.
The story gains new details that no one can source.
Invitations, referrals or opportunities quietly dry up and no reason is ever given.
People who once knew you well start repeating the story as though they had changed their mind about you.
Reputation Laundering.repair_check: When someone realizes the story had no source, repair looks like them going back to the people they told and saying they cannot stand behind it. Telling you privately that they believe you, while leaving the rumor untouched in public, does not take it back out of circulation.
Reputation Laundering.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether the person who repeated the story is willing to say where it came from when you ask. Naming the source and then dropping the claim shows respect for the limit. Changing the subject, or saying they cannot remember, then repeating it, shows the reverse.
Reputation Laundering.psychological_mechanism: Hearing a story several times, from several mouths, can make it seem more believable, even when all the mouths share one origin. Each person who passes it on can also feel entitled to, because others did first. The source drops out of view while the confidence goes up, so the story starts to seem settled.
Reputation Laundering.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe walking into rooms where the verdict has arrived first, feeling they have to prove a negative, and being unable to find anyone to argue with. Some pull back from groups to avoid the looks. Others spend months trying to trace a rumor to its start.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the person repeating it one calm question: 'Who told you that, and did they see it themselves?' Let the answer, or the lack of one, speak.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to discuss the rumor with people who cannot say what they witnessed: 'I will talk about what happened with anyone who was there.'
response_options.disengagement: Step back from the circle that circulates the story, and put your effort into relationships where people deal with you directly.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell one or two people who know you well what is being said, and ask whether they have heard it, who from, and what they make of it.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask your manager to name specific incidents or complaints in writing, and keep a dated record of positive work, feedback and who has seen it.

Reputation Laundering.boundary_script: "I'd like to deal with what actually happened. If you saw something, tell me what it was. If you only heard it from others, please don't pass it on as fact, and I'm glad to answer anything you want to ask me directly."
Reputation Laundering.safety_note: Reputation laundering is usually painful but not dangerous. It becomes serious when the rumor costs you your job, housing, custody or standing in a community, or when it is used to justify harassment. Keep dated records and screenshots, and take them to an employment adviser, a union rep or legal aid service.
misuse_warning: Calling a legitimate warning from several people 'laundering' can wave away real concerns about someone's conduct.
The label should not be used to demand that others stay silent about their own first-hand experience.
Reputation Laundering.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Information cascades describe how a belief spreads because agreeing feels safer, and nobody has to have planted it. Reputation laundering is narrower: it concerns a claim about one person, and the missing source is the point. Gatekeeping uses the resulting reputation to decide who gets access. Punishment by proxy hurts someone you care about; laundering hurts you through what others believe.
Reputation Laundering.core_meaning: Passing a damaging or flattering claim about a person through enough retellings that it loses its source and starts to feel like common knowledge.

Maternal Gatekeeping.short_definition: A mother's habit of correcting, redoing or limiting the other parent's or caregiver's care of a child until they lose confidence and step back.
Maternal Gatekeeping.expanded_definition: Maternal gatekeeping is a term from family research for the ways a mother, often without noticing, can limit how much another caregiver does with a child, usually the father but sometimes a grandparent or stepparent. It includes redoing tasks, giving instructions about methods with no single right way, and being the one who decides who may care for the child. One correction about safety is ordinary. The pattern is when competent care keeps being redone and the other caregiver slowly stops trying.
Maternal Gatekeeping.plain_language_summary: One parent keeps correcting or redoing how the other one cares for the child, until the second parent gives up and does less, which then seems to prove they were not capable.
Maternal Gatekeeping.why_this_matters: The corrected caregiver's confidence erodes until they step back, and the stepping back is then read as proof they were never really willing. Both the child and that caregiver can lose time and closeness.
what_it_is: Re-doing a task right after the other caregiver finishes it: re-dressing the baby, re-packing the bag, re-washing the bottle.
Giving detailed rules about things with many working methods, such as bath order or how to hold a baby.
Controlling the calendar, so the other caregiver gets care time only when the gatekeeper allows it.
Criticizing in front of the child or other relatives, so the caregiver is seen as clumsy.
A concept from family studies, not a verdict on any mother. Fathers and other caregivers can also gate.
what_it_sounds_like: No, give her to me, you're holding her wrong.
I'll just do it, it's quicker than explaining.
You did put his socks on inside out. I'll fix it.
Don't take her to the park without me, you don't know her signals.
That's not how we do bedtime. Here, let me.
You can babysit him on Saturday, but I've written down exactly what to do.
He only settles for me, so there's no point you trying.
what_it_is_not: One specific safety concern, raised constructively, is not this. Examples are a sleeping position, a car seat strap or an allergy.
Two caregivers can have genuinely different methods that both work. Choosing one routine for consistency is not control.
Someone still learning a skill can be given proportionate guidance without their competence being the target.
A breastfeeding mother who needs to be the one to settle a baby for practical reasons.
A parent recovering from birth or ill health who is anxious and over-protective, and relaxes once reassured.
A child with medical needs whose care really does require specific steps.
this_may_be_it_when: Tasks on which there is no single right way are corrected or redone most times they are done.
The other caregiver has said they have stopped doing a task because it just gets redone.
The corrections come in front of the child, family or friends.
Access to the child is arranged around the gatekeeper's approval and rules are changed after the fact.
A request to share more of the care meets reasons that never run out.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The parent hands over the task and leaves, even if they would have done it differently.
The corrections are about things that affect safety and stop once the other caregiver knows them.
Both caregivers criticize each other's methods about equally, and also accept it.
The other caregiver has asked for the corrections or the checklist.
The one who corrects is also teaching, and hands over more as skill grows.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A new parent who is exhausted and anxious may hover over everything before trust has had time to build.
A parent who has done most of the care may truly know details, like a child's allergy or routines, that the other has not learned.
Different upbringings give people honest disagreement about what is normal for a child.
common_false_positives: A mother who writes a long note for a first overnight with a medically complex child.
A father who is told to hold a newborn's head, once, and then is left to it.
A grandparent who is asked not to feed a child nuts because of an allergy.
discernment_questions: Is the correction about the child's safety, or about doing it the way the corrector would?
Does the other caregiver get to try a task twice, including when it goes imperfectly?
Have I, or has my partner, noticed that someone has stopped offering to help?
If a task went differently but the child was fine, is it left alone?
Would I accept this level of correcting of my own care from someone else?
less_concerning_if: The corrector steps back once the other caregiver has shown they can do the task safely.
Both caregivers feel their style is wanted and the child is at ease with both.
Differences in method are discussed with curiosity instead of being fixed on the spot.
more_concerning_if: The other caregiver is kept from time alone with the child or from medical and school contacts.
The criticism is used in a custody or family dispute as proof that the caregiver is not capable.
The child is told that only one parent can do things properly.
pattern_over_time_signs: The other caregiver does fewer tasks each month, and the one correcting does more and is more tired.
The corrected caregiver starts asking permission for things they once did on their own.
The child begins to ask for one parent only, and the other is hurt.
Past efforts get remembered as failures: 'You tried, remember how that went'.
Maternal Gatekeeping.repair_check: Once the pattern is raised, repair is the corrector handing over a whole task, such as bedtime, and leaving the room while it is done in a different way. A promise to be 'less critical' that is followed by re-checking each task has not changed what the caregiver experiences.
Maternal Gatekeeping.boundary_respect_check: After you ask to handle a task your own way, ask yourself whether the task stays yours the next time. A boundary that was heard looks like a task left alone, even when it is not done as they would do it. One that was not looks like a quiet redo once you leave.
Maternal Gatekeeping.psychological_mechanism: Repeated correction on tasks without one right answer can teach a caregiver that their own judgment is not trusted, and so they may check with the other parent, or stop trying. The one doing most care may also feel the stakes of the child's wellbeing are carried by them alone, which can make handing over feel risky. Each side's behavior can then reinforce the other's.
Maternal Gatekeeping.possible_impact_on_receiver: People on the receiving end describe feeling like a helper rather than a parent, losing the nerve to make small choices and feeling shut out of the child's routines. Some withdraw to avoid the criticism, and then worry that it looks like not caring. Others feel grief about missed time.

response_options.soft_clarification: Pick one task and say what you would like: 'Can bath time be mine this week, done my way, and we compare notes afterwards on how it went?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask for corrections to be limited to safety: 'If it's about safety, tell me and I'll change it. If it's just a different method, please let it be.'
response_options.disengagement: If a conversation turns into a fight about methods, pause it and return when the child is not in the room, rather than arguing in front of them.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to a pediatric nurse, a parenting group or a family counselor, who can say what is a real safety issue and what is a style choice.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you work with families, for example as a health visitor or teacher, offer both caregivers the same information, and avoid treating one as the default parent.

Maternal Gatekeeping.boundary_script: "I want to be an equal parent to her, and that means doing some things differently from you. If something is a safety issue, say so and I'll listen. If it's just not how you would do it, I'd like to be left to do it my way."
Maternal Gatekeeping.safety_note: This pattern is usually about confidence and closeness, not danger. It would change if access to the child is cut off, if one parent is told they may not see the child, or if control extends to money, phone or movement. In that case, a family lawyer or a domestic abuse advocate can help you see where you stand.
misuse_warning: Using the term against a mother who has a real safety concern, or who is the main carer and is simply tired, turns a research concept into blame.
The label can also be used to dismiss a mother who has legitimate reasons for restricting contact. Gatekeeping needs the pattern, not just the disagreement.
Maternal Gatekeeping.how_to_distinguish_from_related: General gatekeeping controls access to people or resources of any kind; the maternal form is specifically a caregiver's control of another caregiver's role with a child. Interruption patterns cut someone off in group talk; here the cutting off happens through redone and taken-over tasks. Punishment by proxy harms someone you care about to send a message. Here the target is the caregiving role itself, not a message.
Maternal Gatekeeping.core_meaning: A mother's habit of correcting, redoing or limiting the other parent's or caregiver's care of a child until they lose confidence and step back.

Echo Chamber Construction.short_definition: Arranging what another person reads, hears and talks about so that they mostly meet one view, and come to see every other source as unreliable.
Echo Chamber Construction.expanded_definition: An echo chamber is a closed circle in which the same views bounce back and outside voices are cast as biased. Construction is the active part: someone feeds a person selected sources, introduces them to one set of friends, and pre-labels outsiders as liars or fools before they have spoken. Sharing links you like is ordinary. The pattern is when other sources are steadily discouraged, and doubt about outsiders is taught in advance.
Echo Chamber Construction.plain_language_summary: Someone slowly fills your information world with one point of view and teaches you in advance to distrust everyone else, so it feels like your own choice.
Echo Chamber Construction.why_this_matters: The target loses the outside views that would let them sense-check their own situation, and the narrowing arrives feeling like a preference they chose. It is hard to notice what you are no longer hearing.
what_it_is: Steady recommendations of the same few channels, authors or forums, with a dismissal of everything else.
Introducing the person to one circle of friends or one online group, and cooling their ties with others.
Describing outsiders in advance as biased, paid or 'asleep', so their views are discounted before they are heard.
Praise for repeating the group's view, and awkward silence for questions.
It differs from simply liking a community. The marker is discouragement of everything else.
what_it_sounds_like: Don't bother with that site, they're all lying anyway.
Your sister would only confuse you. She doesn't understand what we know.
Here, watch this one. It explains everything the others hide.
If you hear them out, they'll just twist your words.
Real friends would see this the way we do.
You don't need other opinions. You've got us.
Anyone who disagrees hasn't done the research.
what_it_is_not: People form affinity groups on their own, and recommending sources you honestly rate is not curating somebody else's world.
The distinguishing feature is active discouragement of everything else, not enthusiasm for something in particular.
A parent who limits a young child's screen content is making an age-appropriate choice.
A recommendation algorithm that serves more of the same is how the platform works, and this does not show what anyone meant.
A hobby group, faith community or fan club that shares a strong view but welcomes questions and outside friends.
A friend who says a particular source is unreliable and gives their reasons for you to check.
this_may_be_it_when: You are told in advance, in general terms, that certain sources or people cannot be trusted.
Questions about the group's view get hurt reactions or a change of subject.
Your time with other friends and family shrinks as time with the one circle grows.
Information that disagrees is described as an attack before you have read it.
You notice you repeat phrases and examples that you first heard from one person.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The person gives reasons for distrusting a source and invites you to check them yourself.
You keep friends, news sources and interests outside the group and nobody objects.
The group answers hard questions with evidence rather than a mood.
You can describe the best case for a view the group rejects.
Leaving the group or disagreeing with it carries no penalty.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People naturally befriend others who think alike, and the circle narrows without anyone planning it.
Platform recommendations feed you more of what you clicked, with no human steering.
A new enthusiast can sound like a convert for a few months and then settle.
common_false_positives: A new member of a club who spends all their free time with it for a season.
A friend who warns you off a site that has really published false stories.
A family that mostly talks politics with relatives who agree, with no pressure on the others.
discernment_questions: When did I last read or hear a serious case against what this circle thinks?
Who told me those sources could not be trusted, and did they show me why?
Do I still have friends outside this group, and has that changed?
What happens when I voice doubt: curiosity, or coolness?
Could I explain the other side's view well enough that they would recognize it?
less_concerning_if: You choose your own sources and the person is relaxed about it.
Outside friendships and views are welcomed, even if teased.
The group changes its mind when shown good evidence.
more_concerning_if: The person asks you to cut contact with people who disagree, or to delete or avoid certain accounts.
Group membership becomes tied to money, housing or a relationship.
You are told that outside people are dangerous or are out to harm you.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your list of trusted sources keeps getting shorter, and each loss comes with a reason.
You start to finish the group's sentences and use its private vocabulary.
Old friends say you have changed, and you feel defensive before they finish speaking.
Reading something the group frowns on makes your stomach tighten.
Echo Chamber Construction.repair_check: When the narrowing is named, repair looks like the person encouraging you to read widely, backing contact with those you have drifted from, and tolerating your doubts without any penalty. A short pause in the pressure, followed by a return to the same sources and the same warnings, is not that.
Echo Chamber Construction.boundary_respect_check: Try something small, such as saying you will read a source they dislike, or meet an old friend alone. Does the person accept it, or pay you back with sulking, a lecture or sudden coldness? Accepting without a price suggests the limit is being respected.
Echo Chamber Construction.psychological_mechanism: Hearing the same view often, from people you like, can make it feel like plain fact. Having your view echoed back can also feel good. If outsiders are described as biased before they speak, their arguments can be dismissed without being weighed. Over time this can make one circle's picture feel like plain reality, and doubt feel like betrayal.
Echo Chamber Construction.possible_impact_on_receiver: Meeting outsiders can come as a shock, with the world looking different from what the circle said. Some report losing touch with relatives, finding it hard to talk to anyone who disagrees, and feeling embarrassed later about what they once repeated with certainty.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask a mild question when you hear a sweeping claim: 'What is the best argument against that, and where would I read it?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep your own reading and your own friends: 'I'm going to keep seeing my sister and reading more widely, and that doesn't change how I feel about you.'
response_options.disengagement: Reduce time in the closed group chat or forum, and see what changes when you do. Do it quietly, and without a speech.
response_options.support_seeking: Reach out to one person from before and tell them honestly what you have been hearing lately. See whether they remain steady and kind.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If this is a workplace team or professional network, ask for more than one source of information on decisions, and put questions in writing.

Echo Chamber Construction.boundary_script: "I like a lot of what you share, and I also want to hear other views for myself. I'll keep reading widely and keep seeing my friends. If we disagree on something, I'd rather talk it through than be told the other side is lying."
Echo Chamber Construction.safety_note: Echo chamber construction is not by itself a physical-safety signal. It becomes one if you are told to cut off family, hand over passwords or devices, or if leaving the circle brings threats or loss of housing or income. At that point, reach for an outside person you trust, and for a cult-recovery or domestic abuse service.
misuse_warning: Saying someone is 'in an echo chamber' is a quick way to dismiss their view without engaging with it. Everyone's circle is somewhat narrow.
It can be turned on a loved one who has found a community that suits them, when nobody is steering them and the door is open.
Echo Chamber Construction.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Information cascades spread a belief because agreeing seems safe, and no single person has to run it. Echo chamber construction has someone actively shaping the supply and teaching distrust of the rest. Gatekeeping controls who gets in or out, and here the control is over what gets in to your head. Strategic ambiguity is about vague wording; this is about a narrow diet.
Echo Chamber Construction.core_meaning: Arranging what another person reads, hears and talks about so that they mostly meet one view, and come to see every other source as unreliable.

Stochastic Harassment Direction.short_definition: Repeatedly describing a named person in inflammatory terms to a large audience, so some listeners predictably harass them although the speaker never gives an instruction.
Stochastic Harassment Direction.expanded_definition: Stochastic means 'driven by chance': nobody can say which listener will act, only that with a large enough audience, some probably will. In this pattern, someone repeatedly names a target and describes them in a way that provokes anger, often with their workplace or town, and never gives an instruction. Then a wave of messages, calls or visits arrives. One harsh post means little. The pattern is repeated portrayal, followed by repeated waves that cite the same words.
Stochastic Harassment Direction.plain_language_summary: Someone keeps painting a particular person as a villain to a large audience, never telling anyone to do anything, and then strangers start harassing that person.
Stochastic Harassment Direction.why_this_matters: The target absorbs harassment from many people at once while the portrayal that produced it stays technically deniable, so there is no single act to report and no one to hold to it. It can feel as if the whole world has turned on you.
what_it_is: A repeated, inflammatory description of a named individual, often with their job, school or neighbourhood attached.
An audience large and angry enough that a few of its members acting is close to certain.
No direct instruction, only a framing that makes harassment seem justified, so the speaker can say they never asked for it.
Waves of messages, calls or complaints that arrive soon after each post and quote its wording.
It is about foreseeable effect over time, not about one person's anger or one heated post.
what_it_sounds_like: Posts that name the person, say what a disgrace they are, and tag their employer or school.
Followers' messages that quote the speaker's exact phrase: 'You are exactly what he said you are.'
The speaker's reply to complaints: 'I never told anyone to contact her. I only said what she did.'
A flood of one-star reviews, calls to the workplace or anonymous emails within hours of a post.
Repeated hints such as 'someone should do something about this person' with no instruction attached.
The target's address, workplace or family showing up in comments after a post, posted by strangers.
New accounts appearing in the target's inbox with the same few insults.
what_it_is_not: Proportionate public criticism of someone's public actions is legitimate, even when a third party overreacts to it.
Reporting real wrongdoing through proper channels is not incitement.
What is described here is repeated inflammatory portrayal aimed at an audience, not criticism as such.
A single harsh review or angry post that happens to go viral, with no pattern of repeated targeting.
A news outlet reporting accurately on a public figure, and some readers reacting badly.
A group of people independently angry about the same documented event.
this_may_be_it_when: The same person returns to the same target again and again, each time with sharper language.
Waves of harassment follow the speaker's posts closely and quote their phrases.
The speaker names or tags the target's employer, school or home area when it adds nothing to the point being made.
When harassment starts, the speaker disclaims it but keeps going.
Personal details that the speaker never posted begin to circulate among the audience.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The speaker explicitly condemns the harassment and removes or edits the post.
The criticism is about a public act of a public figure, and keeps to that act.
The backlash began before the speaker said anything, from other sources.
The speaker has not referred to the target again since the first post.
The target is a public official or business criticized for what they did in that role.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A writer can be shocked by a post's reach and bewildered by what some readers do with it.
An emotional post written in anger may be regretted, and handled well after a pause.
A story can spread without the original author's input, through other people sharing it.
common_false_positives: A viral complaint about a restaurant that brings in a spike of harsh reviews, with no repeated targeting.
A journalist's report on a politician's record that draws hostile replies.
A reply thread of critics responding to a public statement by a company spokesperson.
discernment_questions: Did the harassment arrive after a specific post, and does it quote that post's words?
Has the speaker returned to this person more than once, and with escalating language?
Did the speaker say anything to calm their audience when the harassment began?
Is the person being named in a way that connects to a public role, or to their private life?
Would the criticism have been just as clear without pointing the audience at their workplace or home?
less_concerning_if: The speaker moves on from the topic, or states plainly that nobody should contact the person.
The criticism concerns something the person did in public, and names no private details.
The reaction is limited to ordinary replies and does not reach the target's work or family.
more_concerning_if: The harassment includes threats, repeated unwanted visits, or the sharing of the person's home address or children's details.
Contact is arriving at the target's workplace, threatening their income.
The speaker keeps posting after the target says they have received threats.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each new burst of harassment follows a new post by a day or two.
The speaker's description gets harsher and the audience's replies get more personal.
New people turn up with the same wording, and the target feels watched in more places.
The target begins to change how they live: locking accounts, varying their routes or leaving their usual places.
Stochastic Harassment Direction.repair_check: If the speaker is confronted with the harassment, repair would be them publicly telling the audience to stop, taking down the posts and not naming the person again. A reply that says 'I never asked anyone to do that' and then goes on posting has changed nothing for the target.
Stochastic Harassment Direction.boundary_respect_check: Ask whether, after you or someone else asks that the posts stop, new waves still follow within days. If the posts stop and the waves die down, the request has been honored. If they continue, then the request is being treated as a part of the story.
Stochastic Harassment Direction.psychological_mechanism: A large audience can contain a few people who are already angry or looking for a target. A vivid, repeated portrayal can tell them whom to be angry at and make acting feel righteous, while the speaker keeps a sense of distance, since no instruction was given. Responsibility then seems to spread out among many senders, and no one feels it entirely.
Stochastic Harassment Direction.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe constant alerts, losing sleep, fear when the phone rings, and pulling out of public life. Some lose work because employers get flooded with complaints. Others describe feeling unable to explain it, since no single message looks serious on its own.

response_options.soft_clarification: If you think you may be the audience, ask yourself in private what the speaker is wanting you to do, and whether you would say it to the person's face.
response_options.firm_boundary: Do not reply to the harassers or to the speaker in public. Block, mute and report from your accounts, and keep screenshots with dates and links.
response_options.disengagement: Lock down accounts, remove personal information from public view, and ask trusted people to help you watch messages so you are not alone with them.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a trusted friend or family member what is happening, and ask for help with a record of each message, including a note of when it arrived.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you are the target at work, tell your manager or HR early, give them your record, and ask that the organization handle calls and emails about you.

Stochastic Harassment Direction.boundary_script: "I am keeping a dated record of every message, and I am not replying to any of them. Will you read through them with me and help me work out who should see them?"
Stochastic Harassment Direction.safety_note: Harassment waves can move from messages to threats, doxxing or visits to a home or workplace. Signs to take seriously are your address being shared, threats naming you or your family, or someone appearing in person. Keep dated copies, report each wave to the platform, and take the file to the police or a victim-support service, who can advise on protective orders.
misuse_warning: Treating any pile-on after a post as proof of orchestrated incitement can shield real wrongdoing from public criticism.
Someone who is being criticized may use the label to cast all criticism of themselves as harassment.
Stochastic Harassment Direction.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Punishment by proxy hits someone the target loves, to send a message, while here the pain lands on the target directly, from many strangers. Information cascades spread a belief because agreeing is safer, and no one aims it at a person. Reputation laundering hides the source of a claim, whereas here the speaker is out in the open and the deniability sits in the lack of any instruction.
Stochastic Harassment Direction.core_meaning: Repeatedly describing a named person in inflammatory terms to a large audience, so some listeners predictably harass them although the speaker never gives an instruction.

Information Laundering.short_definition: Passing a false or unverified claim through a series of apparently credible sources until it looks like established fact and its origin can no longer be seen.
Information Laundering.expanded_definition: Information laundering moves a claim from a weak source, such as an anonymous post or a fabricated document, through a chain of better-looking ones: a blog, a small outlet, a bigger outlet, an expert quoting the outlet. Each step cites the one before and adds a little respectability. Citing earlier reporting is normal. The pattern is when no link in the chain ever checked the claim itself, and the original source fades out of view.
Information Laundering.plain_language_summary: A shaky claim is passed from one source to a more respectable one, and then another, until it looks well-sourced even though nobody ever checked whether it was true.
Information Laundering.why_this_matters: The target is contradicted by something that now looks well-sourced, and disproving it means unpicking a chain of citations rather than a single claim. By then, the claim has been quoted in so many places that it feels settled.
what_it_is: A claim moved upward through outlets of rising credibility, each citing the last.
A circle of sources that repeat each other, so the number of citations looks like independent confirmation.
A weak original, such as a forged document or an anonymous post, that becomes hard to find once better-known outlets carry it.
Credibility gained from the messenger's reputation, not from any new evidence.
It happens in news, in academic citations, in company reports and in word-of-mouth.
what_it_sounds_like: A headline that says 'according to reports' and links to another article that says the same.
A footnote that cites a blog, which cites a forum post, which cites nothing.
An expert on a panel quoting 'a widely reported figure' that cannot be traced to a study.
A news story built on a screenshot that no one has authenticated.
A statistic that appears in many places, all with the same rounding, and none with the underlying data.
An article that is later cited as a source by the site that supplied the original tip.
A correction posted at the original place that does not follow the claim to the places it spread.
what_it_is_not: Responsible journalism legitimately cites and builds on other credible reporting.
A claim that several outlets each confirmed separately is corroborated rather than laundered.
The thing to trace is whether any link in the chain did original verification work.
A well-known idea being cited in a textbook that has itself been properly checked.
An honest error that spreads because busy reporters trusted a reputable source that was wrong.
A source quoting an unnamed person whom the outlet has vetted and stands behind.
this_may_be_it_when: Following the citations ends in a single anonymous or unverifiable origin.
Every source uses the same wording or the same image, and none adds its own checking.
The claim gets more certain at each step, though no new evidence enters.
The earliest source quietly disappears or gets edited once bigger outlets carry the claim.
People who try to trace it find that the sources only point to each other.
this_may_not_be_it_when: One or more sources in the chain interviewed witnesses, checked records or ran their own analysis.
Independent outlets with different sources arrived at the same claim.
The original source is clearly named and has a track record of accuracy.
Corrections traveled with the claim when a mistake was found.
The claim is tentative at every step, and stays that way.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Time pressure leads reputable editors to trust a wire service or partner without redoing the work.
Authors cite secondary sources because the primary one is hard to reach, and say so.
A mistake in one respected outlet may be copied by others in good faith.
common_false_positives: A science story that cites an earlier news report on a peer-reviewed paper, with a link to the paper.
A rumor in a group chat that turns out to be true because a local reporter confirmed it.
An encyclopedia entry that summarizes several independent studies.
discernment_questions: If I follow each citation back, where does it end, and is that source something I can check?
Did any of these sources add new evidence, or did they each repeat the one before?
Is the original easy to find, or has it been hard to locate since the claim spread?
Do the sources disagree in the details in ways that suggest independent work?
Who benefits from this claim being widely believed?
less_concerning_if: Each source names where it got the claim and links to it.
At least one source in the chain shows its evidence, such as documents or recordings.
Outlets that got it wrong issued visible corrections.
more_concerning_if: The claim concerns a named person or group, and has led to threats, firing or harassment.
The origin appears to be a forged document, edited image or fake account.
Outlets refuse to say where the claim came from when asked.
pattern_over_time_signs: The same unverified claim returns months later, now with a longer list of citations.
Search results fill with articles that quote each other and none the original source.
Attempts to correct the record are answered with 'it has been widely reported'.
Details of the claim harden over time, such as numbers becoming exact, while the evidence stays thin.
Information Laundering.repair_check: When a chain is exposed, repair looks like each outlet stating that it relied on an earlier source it did not check, updating the original piece and telling readers who saw the earlier version. Quietly deleting a link while leaving the claim in place does not remove it from circulation.
Information Laundering.boundary_respect_check: When you ask an outlet or colleague where a claim came from, watch how they respond. Naming the source and conceding what they did not check shows that the question was respected. Pointing to the number of other places that ran it avoids the question.
Information Laundering.psychological_mechanism: Messenger reputation often does the work that checking should. Readers can judge a claim by how reputable the messenger seems and by how often they have seen it, rather than checking the root. A respectable outlet can lend its reputation to something it did not verify. Seeing a claim in several places can feel like confirmation, even when they all trace to one origin.
Information Laundering.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe the frustration of facing a claim that seems sourced and cannot be answered in one line. Targets report harm to their name or job from something they never said. Readers describe feeling foolish on learning that the 'many sources' were one.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the person sharing it: 'Where does this first come from, before the article?' Wait for an answer you can check.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to repeat or cite the claim until you have traced it to a source that did its own checking.
response_options.disengagement: Stop engaging with a thread that is only citing itself, and avoid sharing it further, which gives it more reach.
response_options.support_seeking: Send the chain you traced to a fact-checking organization, a librarian or a reporter who covers the topic, and ask them to review it.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you edit, research or cite for work, require a primary source for key claims and note in your records how each source was checked.

Information Laundering.boundary_script: Verification script (to yourself, before sharing): "Can I trace this back to someone who actually saw it, measured it or held the document? Or am I looking at five sources that all got it from the same place?"
Information Laundering.safety_note: Information laundering is mostly a harm to understanding and reputation. It becomes a safety matter if a laundered claim names a private person and prompts harassment, threats or loss of work. If that happens, save copies of the pages, report to the platforms and outlets, and speak to a lawyer or a media-law advice service.
misuse_warning: Calling a claim 'laundered' just because you dislike it, without tracing it, dismisses honest reporting.
The label can be used to wave away any claim that many outlets carried, even when each one verified it separately.
Information Laundering.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Information cascades spread a claim because agreeing is safer, and nobody needs to have staged the climb. Information laundering is built to make a weak claim look verified, and the chain matters. Strategic ambiguity keeps meaning vague to avoid being pinned down, while here the claim is specific but its origin is hidden. Reputation laundering does the same to a person's image.
Information Laundering.core_meaning: Passing a false or unverified claim through a series of apparently credible sources until it looks like established fact and its origin can no longer be seen.
